parts.title: Structured prompting
parts.outcome: I tell the AI clearly what I need, so it guesses less and gives steadier answers.

skip.teaches: How to tell your AI clearly what you need, how to name what a first attempt leaves out, and how to rewrite it with a framework.
skip.matters: Clear instructions make answers steadier, and steadier answers are the only kind you can check with rules.

ui.map_aria: Course map. You are at Part {n} of {total}.
ui.finished_body: Your work is saved in your project folder: your two prompts, their answers and the prompt you rewrote from your own work. You can now explain why giving the AI a structure gets better results, and you can use a framework or build your own. In Part 2 you turn "that looks good" into clear pass or fail rules. Reviews will still appear here when they are due.

parts.title: Defining evaluation criteria
parts.outcome: I turn "that looks good" into clear pass or fail rules.

skip.teaches: How to turn "that looks good" into separate criteria, give each one a pass or fail threshold a script could decide, and write them down as test cases.
skip.matters: A rule you cannot test cannot be checked. These test cases are what the checker in the next Part is built from.

ui.map_aria: Course map. You are at Part {n} of {total}.
ui.finished_body: Your work is saved in your project folder: your worksheet and your test cases in part-2{sep}test-cases.md. You can now turn what you need from an answer into distinct criteria, give each one a pass or fail threshold a script could decide, and record them as test cases. In Part 3 an AI agent turns a file like this into a checker and runs it on real answers. The Practice task is for practice only and is not something to submit. Reviews will still appear here when they are due.

parts.title: Running evals and baseline
parts.outcome: I check five AI answers against my rules and record a starting score.

skip.teaches: How your AI builds a checker from your test cases, how to check that the checker can be trusted, and how to run it on five answers and record a starting score.
skip.matters: Without a checker you can trust and a starting score, you cannot tell whether a change to your prompt made things better or worse.

parts.title: Iterating with evaluation-driven development
parts.outcome: I change my prompt, check again with the same rules and see whether the score moved.

parts.title: Load-bearing audit and packaging
parts.outcome: I keep only the instructions that earn their place and package my work so someone else can use it.

parts.title: Your own task
parts.outcome: A live working meeting. You choose a task of your own that repeats, has clear requirements and can be checked by rules, and talk your ideas through with the others.

ui.intro: Is it good enough to use? How do you know? An evaluated system answers both: it is asked for clearly, judged against rules you can test, measured so that a better prompt is a fact and not an opinion, and kept to what earns its place. Below is where you learn to do each of these, ending with a task of your own.
